data.content_ref: inline:The target's central claim is that Popper's preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible 'on his own terms' as a non-inductive methodological rule grounded in verisimilitude. But the target provides no derivation (the derivation array is empty) and no formalization (formalization_refs is empty) linking corroboration to verisimilitude. The mechanism states that corroboration 'reports past performance without predicting future success (blocking induction),' yet simultaneously asserts the preference is 'aimed at maximizing verisimilitude.' This is the fatal gap: verisimilitude is a truth-directed notion (how close a theory is to the truth), and to claim that choosing the most-corroborated theory maximizes verisimilitude requires treating past corroboration as evidence of present truth-likeness. That move IS induction — precisely what the target claims to avoid. The target cannot simultaneously hold that corroboration has no predictive bearing on a theory's truth-status (blocking induction) and that corroboration guides us toward greater truth-likeness (verisimilitude). If corroboration is epistemically inert regarding truth, then 'maximizing verisimilitude' via corroboration is unmotivated within Popper's own anti-inductive framework. The target's own countercondition concedes this: if the Miller-Tichý refutation holds, 'the bridge between corroboration and truth-likeness collapses, rendering the preference arbitrary within Popper's logic.' But the target never establishes that the bridge stands independently of induction — it merely asserts it. Thus the claim of non-inductive defensibility 'on his own terms' is unearned: the argument smuggles in the very inductive inference it disavows.
